text: Before Sentinel can show you a single alert, it needs somewhere to put the data. This lesson is about that somewhere — the Log Analytics workspace — and why understanding it changes how you'll think about everything else in this course, starting with KQL in the very next chapter.

A Log Analytics workspace is a real Azure resource, part of Azure Monitor Logs, and it exists independently of Sentinel — it's used across Azure for all kinds of log and telemetry storage, not just security. When you 'enable Sentinel,' what you're actually doing is turning on Sentinel's security capabilities on top of a workspace that lives in a specific subscription, resource group, and region, with its own name and its own access controls.

Here's the mental model that matters most: Sentinel does not store its own, separate copy of your data. Every log and every event that flows into Sentinel is a row written into a table inside that Log Analytics workspace. Sentinel's incident queue, its analytics rules, its hunting pages — all of it reads from and writes to that same underlying workspace, directly, the same way a KQL query like this one does.

Inside the workspace, data lands in named tables — SigninLogs for Entra ID sign-in events, SecurityEvent for Windows security events, OfficeActivity for Microsoft 365 activity, CommonSecurityLog for CEF-formatted data from firewalls and other devices. Each data connector you turn on, which the next lesson covers, is really just a pipe writing into one or more of these specific tables.

Understanding the workspace changes how you think about three things you'll run into constantly. Every KQL query you write runs directly against this workspace, with no separate Sentinel-only query layer. Access control is enforced largely at the workspace level through Azure role-based access control. And cost and retention, covered in Lesson 4, are billed and configured at the workspace level, not per individual Sentinel feature.

Most organizations run one workspace per Sentinel deployment, though large enterprises and managed security providers sometimes split data across multiple workspaces by business unit or customer. Next: data connectors, the actual pipes that decide which logs land in which of these tables in the first place.
